lead: A turbocharger is a turbine driven by exhaust gas that spins a compressor and pushes more air into the engine. The exhaust energy is otherwise wasted, so the power seems free. The catch is time: the turbine and compressor have mass, and they take a moment to speed up. That delay is turbo lag. Turbochargers are common on small petrol and diesel cars, tractors and trucks, where more air means more fuel burnt and more power from a smaller engine.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.5 for pressure ratio and density ratio, and Unit 5 for air flow measurement.

sections.h3: Layout and the two turbocharging methods

blocks.text: A turbocharger has a turbine wheel and a compressor wheel on one shaft, held in a bearing housing. Hot exhaust gas enters the turbine housing, pushes the turbine wheel, and leaves through the exhaust pipe. The shaft spins the compressor wheel, which draws air through the air filter and pushes it into the intake manifold at higher pressure and density. The bearing housing gets pressurised oil from the engine; the oil film supports the shaft and carries heat away from the hot turbine end. A wastegate is a valve that lets some exhaust gas bypass the turbine, and its actuator sets how much boost the engine makes.

The energy comes from exhaust enthalpy, not from the air. Exhaust at high pressure and temperature still has work to give, and the turbine extracts it. That is why a turbocharger is called an exhaust-driven supercharger.

Two manifold methods are common. In constant-pressure turbocharging, all cylinders feed one exhaust manifold. The pulses mix and the turbine sees an almost steady pressure. This suits steady high-load running, but at low load the pulses are lost in the volume and response is slow. In pulse turbocharging, narrow pipes keep the exhaust pulses separate and aim them at the turbine. The pulse energy arrives quickly, so boost builds earlier. Most road vehicles use pulse turbocharging.

A single turbo must work from low to rated speed, so its size is a compromise. Twin turbos can be parallel: two small turbos, each feeding half the cylinders. Smaller wheels have less inertia, so they spin up faster. Twin turbos can also be in series: a small turbo makes boost at low speed, a large turbo takes over at high speed, and valves switch the flow. A crank-driven blower, covered in Chapter 4.5, gives boost as soon as the engine turns, but it takes power from the crankshaft.

sections.h3: Boost threshold is not turbo lag

blocks.text: Boost threshold is the lowest engine speed, at a given load, where the exhaust flow can spin the turbine fast enough for the compressor to exceed atmospheric pressure. Below the threshold the turbo is a restriction, not a boost source. A large turbine housing raises the threshold; a small one lowers it. The threshold is a speed.

Turbo lag is a time. Open the throttle at a speed above the threshold and the boost does not appear at once. The exhaust gas must first accelerate the turbine wheel, shaft and compressor wheel; the intake pipes and intercooler must then fill with denser air. A typical small petrol turbo takes about one to two seconds to reach full boost after a throttle step. The figure shows this: throttle moves in the first 0.3 s, the turbine spools from 0.2 s to 1.5 s, and full boost arrives at about 1.6 s.

Lag is felt as a pause followed by a surge. It is worst after a gear change or when the engine has been cruising at low load. The cure is not more boost; it is less rotating mass, a smaller turbine housing, or split exhaust pulses.

Matching a turbocharger means choosing a compressor and turbine that work well together over the engine range. On the compressor side, the operating point at cruise should sit inside the high-efficiency island, typically 70 to 75 percent, away from surge at low flow and choke at high flow. On the turbine side, the shaft speed must stay below its limit at rated power. A wastegate protects the turbine: when boost reaches the set value, the actuator opens the wastegate and bypasses exhaust around the turbine. Less exhaust through the turbine means less turbine power, so boost stops rising. The actuator can be a spring-and-diaphragm can or an electronic motor.

Anti-lag measures attack inertia and exhaust volume. A small turbine housing raises gas velocity at low flow, at the cost of exhaust backpressure at high flow. A twin-scroll turbine housing keeps the pulses from cylinders that would otherwise interfere; pairing cylinders so their exhaust events are evenly spaced gives each pulse a clear path to the wheel. Lightweight turbine and compressor wheels, and ball bearings instead of journal bearings, cut the rotating mass and friction. Variable geometry, covered in Chapter 4.7, changes the turbine nozzle area with speed.

Heat soak is the other habit. After a hard run, the turbine housing is hot. If the engine stops at once, oil flow stops, and the oil left in the bearing housing can cook into carbon, damaging the bearing and shaft seal. Idling for a minute or two lets oil carry heat away. Modern water-cooled bearing housings reduce this risk, but the habit is still useful.

figure.caption: The throttle bar moves first; the boost bar stays short until the turbine has spun up. The gap between the throttle bar and the full-boost bar is the lag the driver feels.

spec.aria: Timeline showing the throttle opened at zero, the turbine spooling up over the next second, and boost becoming full only after about 1.6 seconds.

examples.question: A 2 litre four-stroke engine runs at 3000 rpm. Intake air density is 1.2 kg/m³. The compressor raises the air temperature by 62 K. Take cp for air as 1.005 kJ/kg·K. Exhaust mass flow is 0.062 kg/s, cp for exhaust gas is 1.15 kJ/kg·K, and the turbocharger mechanical efficiency is 0.65. Find the compressor power and the required exhaust temperature drop across the turbine.
steps: Swept volume per intake stroke = 2 × 10⁻³ m³. A four-stroke engine has one intake stroke per two revolutions, so at 3000 rpm there are 3000/2 = 1500 intake strokes per minute.
Volume flow of air Q = 2 × 10⁻³ m³ × 1500 / 60 = 0.050 m³/s.
Air mass flow m_a = density × Q = 1.2 kg/m³ × 0.050 m³/s = 0.060 kg/s.
Compressor power P_c = m_a cp_a ΔT_a = 0.060 kg/s × 1.005 kJ/kg·K × 62 K = 3.74 kW.
Turbine must supply more than this because of mechanical loss: P_t = P_c / η_m = 3.74 kW / 0.65 = 5.75 kW.
Turbine power also equals m_exh cp_g ΔT_t. So ΔT_t = P_t / (m_exh cp_g) = 5.75 kW / (0.062 kg/s × 1.15 kJ/kg·K) = 80.7 K.
examples.answer: Compressor power is 3.74 kW, and the exhaust gas must drop by about 81 K across the turbine.
examples.check:
Vd = 2e-3
rpm = 3000
rho = 1.2
Q = Vd * (rpm / 2) / 60
m_dot_air = rho * Q
cp_a = 1.005
dT_a = 62
P_c = m_dot_air * cp_a * dT_a
m_dot_exh = 0.062
cp_g = 1.15
eta_m = 0.65
P_t = P_c / eta_m
dT_t = P_t / (m_dot_exh * cp_g)
print(round(Q, 2))
print(round(m_dot_air, 2))
print(round(P_c, 2))
print(round(dT_t, 1))

traps: Lag and boost threshold get mixed up. Threshold is a speed below which no boost is possible; lag is a time delay at a speed where boost is possible.
The turbo does not run on air. It runs on exhaust enthalpy, which includes both pressure and temperature.
The wastegate bypasses exhaust around the turbine. It does not dump intake air, and it does not open the compressor side.
A large turbine housing lowers exhaust backpressure at high power but raises the boost threshold. A small housing spools quickly but can choke the top end.
Boost is often given in bar gauge while pressure ratio is absolute. At sea level, 1.0 bar gauge means pressure ratio about 2.0, not 1.0.

quiz.q: Name the main parts of a turbocharger and state the function of the bearing housing.
quiz.a: Turbine wheel, compressor wheel, shaft, bearing housing, turbine housing, compressor housing, wastegate and actuator. The bearing housing holds the shaft in an oil film and carries heat away from the turbine end.

quiz.q: Why does pulse turbocharging give better low-speed response than constant-pressure turbocharging?
quiz.a: Pulse turbocharging keeps the exhaust pulses separate in narrow pipes and aims them at the turbine. The pulse energy arrives quickly. Constant-pressure turbocharging mixes all pulses in one manifold, so the turbine sees a steadier but lower-energy flow at low load and response is slower.

quiz.q: A turbocharger gives 0.8 bar gauge boost at sea level where atmospheric pressure is 1.0 bar. Find the compressor pressure ratio.
quiz.a: Absolute outlet pressure = 1.0 + 0.8 = 1.8 bar. Pressure ratio = 1.8 / 1.0 = 1.8.

quiz.q: A driver says the car has no power below 1800 rpm but pulls strongly after 2000 rpm. Is this lag or boost threshold? Explain.
quiz.a: It is mainly the boost threshold. Below about 1800 rpm the exhaust flow cannot spin the turbine enough to make boost, so the engine feels weak. Lag is the delay after a throttle step above that speed.

quiz.q: A wastegate actuator is stuck closed. What happens at high engine speed and load?
quiz.a: The wastegate cannot bypass exhaust, so turbine speed and boost keep rising. The compressor may exceed its speed limit, charge air gets very hot, and the engine may knock or suffer high cylinder pressure. In the worst case the turbo or engine is damaged.

quiz.q: Why is it useful to idle for a minute before switching off a hot turbocharged engine?
quiz.a: Idling keeps oil flowing through the bearing housing while the turbine housing cools slightly. If the engine stops at once, oil trapped in the hot bearing housing can cook into carbon and damage the bearing and seal.

quiz.q: How does a twin-scroll turbine housing reduce turbo lag?
quiz.a: It separates the exhaust from cylinders whose pulses would interfere. Each pulse reaches the turbine wheel with more energy and less mixing, so the wheel spins up faster at low speed. It also keeps the exhaust pulses from cancelling each other before the wheel.

quiz.q: State one advantage of a crank-driven blower over a turbocharger.
quiz.a: A crank-driven blower gives boost as soon as the engine turns, so there is almost no lag. Its boost rises with engine speed, not with exhaust energy.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production engines increasingly use electric assist to spin the turbo shaft before exhaust energy is available. Mild-hybrid systems can power such a compressor directly. Engineers also use model-based control to predict boost from throttle and exhaust temperature. Search next for turbocharger matching, compressor map, twin-scroll turbine and electric supercharger.
